jagatī
------------------------------------------
In the वेदस्, छन्दस् or metre, has been given great importance. While reciting a मन्त्र, one of the three factors to be remembered and honoured is the छन्दस्.
Among the well-known Vedic metres, जगती is also one. It has twelve syllables per line and four lines in a stanza. Fifteen varieties of this meter have been mentioned in the works on poetry of the classical period.
Indravaṁśā, toṭaka, bhujaṅga-prayāta, vaṁśasthavila and sragviṇī are the more common varieties.
The general terrace or platform on which a Hindu temple stands is also called ‘jagatī’. The word means in Sanskrit, earth or a world.
See also CHANDAS.

-1670)
------------------------------------------
Author of a well-known work on Sanskrit poetics, the Rasagaṅgādhara, जगन्नाथ पण्डित was the son of Perubhaṭṭa and लक्ष्मी. He belonged to Andhra Pradesh but spent most of his life in North India.
He was the court pundit of Jehāṅgīr and Ṣāhjehān. It was probably the latter who gave him the honorific ‘paṇḍitarāja’ (‘the king of scholars’).
Some of his well-known works are: Viṣṇulaharī, Gaṅgālaharī, Sudhālaharī, Amṛtalaharī and Lakṣmīlaharī.
Unfortunately, the Rasagaṅgādhara is an incomplete work.

Jagaddhātrī pūjā
(‘worship of the [Mother] who is the supporter of the world’)
------------------------------------------
Goddess Jagad-dhātrī (one who is the supporter and nourisher of the world) is widely worshipped by the शाक्त devotees, especially in Bengal and the neighbouring regions. She nourishes the world by providing the fourfold objectives (dharma, अर्थ, काम and मोक्ष, the four puru-ṣārthas) (See PURUṢĀRTHAS.) to mankind. She pervades the three phases of the day and is worshipped in three different ways: the sāttvika mode in the morning, the rājasa mode in the afternoon and the tāmasa mode in the evening.
According to the Kātyāyanītantra (paṭala 76) she appeared as a huge mass of brilliant light in front of इन्द्र and other gods, striking terror in their hearts, since they had become arrogant and vain due to their prowess. When they felt humbled, the mass of light transformed itself into the form of the goddess Jagad-dhātrī.
The deity is described as seated on the back of a lion which is standing on the body of Karīndrāsura (elephant-demon). She is richly dressed with red garments and bedecked with all ornaments. She has four hands carrying शङ्ख (conch), चक्र (discus), धनुस् (bow) and बाण (arrow). She has three eyes and wears a serpent as the उपवीत (sacred thread). Her body is shining like the morning sun.
Her पूजा or special worship falls on Kārttika śukla navamī (the ninth day of the bright half of the month of Kārttika, usually in November). The worship is offered to a clay image specially prepared for the occasion and later immersed in a river or lake or a big tank.

. In Chandannagar, the public pūjās of Jagad-dhātrī draw large crowds.

Jagannātha-Purī
------------------------------------------
One of the celebrated places of पिल्ग्रिमगे for the Hindus since centuries is the जगन्नाथ-पुरी or पुरी in the modern Orissa state. It is situated at a distance of 477 kms. (310 miles) from Calcutta and is on the eastern sea-shore. Bhubaneshvar, the capital of Orissa, is just 60 kms. (36 miles) away.
The famous temple of Jagannātha stands on a gentle slope known as Nīlācala or Nīlaparvata in the पुराणस् and the धर्मशास्त्रस्.
पुरी.jpg" src="http://eoh.rkmathbangalore.org/public/images/thumbs/Jagann%C4%81tha-Pur%C4%AB.jpg" alt="Jagannātha Temple">Jagannātha TempleThe temple town is also called ‘Puruṣottamatīrtha.’
Sometimes a verse from the Ṛgveda (10.155.3) is quoted to support the theory that this place with its temple of wooden images, is a very ancient centre of पिल्ग्रिमगे.
Paurāṇic accounts declare that इन्द्र-dyumna, the pious king of the Mālava country with his capital at Avantī (modern उज्जयिनी) came here and built the temple at the command of Lord वासुदेव (Kṛṣṇa). The wooden images of कृष्ण, बलराम and सुभद्रा were prepared by the heavenly architect विश्वकर्म himself. Though the king had been specially instructed not to look at the working on the images by विश्वकर्म, he did so, unable to control the temptation. Hence Viśva-कर्म left the images unfinished and retired to हेअवेन्. This is the explanation given by the traditional lore for the half-finished images now worshipped in the temple.
Oriental scholars are of the opinion that this holy place with कृष्ण worship (including the use of the wooden images in the shrine) is quite ancient though Buddhist influence reigned supreme for some time before the 5th century A. D.
The centre of attraction of this place is the temple of Lord Jagannātha. The enclosure of the temple is almost a square, 196 metres (652 ft.) by 190 metres (632 ft.) with a massive stone wall 6 metres (20 ft.) high. The विमान or central tower over the sanctum is 58 metres (192 ft.) high. There is a large gate-way on each side of the enclosure, the one on the east (siṁhadvāra) being the best.
There are almost 120 temples dedicated to various aspects of God like शिव, देवी, सूर्य and others, in this enclosure.
The main shrine of पुरुषोत्तम is very ancient. Kings like Coḍagaṅga (A.

) added other structures during their reign.
In the main temple there are four chambers: bhogamandira (hall of offerings), nāṭamandira (hall of dance and मुसिच्), jaganmohanamandira (hall of pilgrims, where the pilgrims can assemble) and the garbhamandira (inner sanctuary).
The जगन्नाथ तेम्प्ले has a large contingent of attendants, divided into 36 orders and 97 classes. At the head, is the राजा of Khurda who calls himself ‘the sweeper of Jagannātha’.
The greatest event of the temple is the temple-car festival, known as the ‘Rathayātrā’. It starts on आषाढ śukla dvitīyā, (2nd day of the bright fortnight of आषाढ, usually in July) and ends on the daśamī (tenth) day of the same fortnight. (See RATHAYĀTRĀ for details.)
The other major festival is the ‘Snānayātrā’ (bathing procession) conducted on the Jyeṣṭha Pūrṇimā (full-मोओन् day in Jyeṣṭha, generally in June) when the three images are brought out on to a platform and anointed by 108 pitchers of sacred water. (See SNĀNAYĀTRĀ also.)
The wooden images are usually replaced by similar ones every twelve years. This is called ‘Navakalevara’ (new body). Some relics (believed to be those of कृष्ण) are transferred from the old images into the new ones.
One special feature of this temple is that caste barriers have been given the go-by.
Śaṅkara (A.

-820) has established one of his four chief monasteries in पुरी. It is called ‘Govardhana मठ’ or ‘Govardhana पीठ’.
Rāmānuja (A.
-1137) had visited this sacred place. So also कबीर् (A.

-1533) lived here for quite a long time and was closely associated with the temple and the king Pratāparudra of Orissa.
In पुरी also five tīrthas or holy places are mentioned, which every pilgrim is expected to visit. They are: the pool of मार्कण्डेय, the Vaṭa tree, बलराम, the sea and the pool of इन्द्रद्युम्न.

-1809) (‘servant of the Lord of the world’)
------------------------------------------
The Haridāsas (‘servants of God’) of Karnataka have carved for themselves an important place in the भक्ति Movement that helped the rejuvenation of हिन्दुइस्म् in medieval India. The four, most important, of these are: पुरन्दरदास, विजय-dāsa, Gopāladāsa and जगन्नाथदास.
His original name was Śrīnivāsā-cārya. Though born in a small village called Byāgavaṭṭe near Mānavi in the Raichur district of Karnataka, he lived most of the time in the latter place. His होउसे has now been converted into his shrine.
Śrīnivāsācārya was a born genius in composing poems in Sanskrit. In course of time he acquired astounding scholarship in the scriptures, especially of the द्वैत school of मध्वाचार्य (A.
-1276). Arrogance of scholarship made him slight विजयदास (A.

-1755) as a result of which he contacted a severe disease of the stomach. By divine intervention he was directed to go to विजयदास himself for succour. विजयदास sent him to his own disciple Gopāladāsa who not only cured him but also initiated him into the Order of the Haridāsas christening him as ‘Jagannātha-Viṭṭhaladāsa’ or, more popularly, ‘Jagannāthadāsa’. This was in A.

.
Jagannāthadāsa has composed many works, the magnum opus being the Śrīharikathāmṛtasāra which he is said to have completed in his 82nd year! It is a voluminous poetical composition of a thousand verses in Kannada, in the meter called ‘bhāminīṣaṭpadī’. He has also composed more than seven hundred songs—both devotional and didactic—in the Kannada language.
His biographers have credited him with many psychic and supernatural powers.
See also DĀSAKŪṬA.
